[[Futsunushi]]
[[Ame no Koyane]]
Himegami | founded_by = | established = 768 | date_destroyed = | location = 160 Kasugano-chō, [[Nara, Nara|Nara-shi]], [[Nara Prefecture|Nara-ken]] | website = {{URL|http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = [[Kasuga-zukuri]] | festival = Kasuga-no-matsuri
(Kasuga-sai: 春日祭) (13th March) | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Kasuga Grand Shrine'''|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in the [[Cities of Japan|city]] of [[Nara, Nara|Nara]], in [[Nara prefecture|Nara Prefecture]], [[Japan]].Richard, Ponsonby-Fane. (1964) '' Visiting Famous Shrines in Japan,'' pp. 221-251. Established in 768 CE and rebuilt several times over the centuries, it is the shrine of the [[Fujiwara family]]. The interior is famous for its many bronze lanterns, as well as the many [[Tōrō|stone lantern]]s that lead up the shrine. The architectural style ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]]'' takes its name from Kasuga Shrine's ''[[honden]]'' (sanctuary). Kasuga Shrine, and the '''Kasugayama Primeval Forest''' near it, are registered as a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] as part of the "[[Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara]]". The path to Kasuga Shrine passes through Deer Park. In Deer Park, deer are able to roam freely and are believed to be sacred messengers of the Shinto gods that inhabit the shrine and surrounding mountainous terrain. Kasuga Shrine and the deer have been featured in several paintings and works of art of the [[Nambokucho Period]].{{cite book|last=[[Birmingham Museum of Art]]|title=Birmingham Museum of Art : guide to the collection|year=2010|publisher=Birmingham Museum of Art|location=[Birmingham, Ala]|isbn=978-1-904832-77-5|pages=46|url=http://artsbma.org}} Over three thousand stone lanterns line the way. The [[Manyo Botanical Garden, Nara|Man'yo Botanical Garden, Nara]] is adjacent to the shrine. == History == === Origin === The birth of this shrine, according to legend, began when the first kami of Kasuga-taisha, [[Takemikazuchi]], rode on the back of a white deer to the top of [[Mount Wakakusa|Mount Mikasa]] in 768 CE.{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|first=Royall|last=Tyler|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} This kami is said to have traveled from the [[Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingu Shrine]] in order to protect [[Nara]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|title=Main Sanctuary|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} The shrine location first received favor from the Imperial government in the [[Heian period]] as a result of the power from the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara family]] as well as [[Empress Shotoku]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/index.html|title=世界遺産 春日大社 公式ホームページ|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} From 1871 through 1946, Kasuga Shrine was officially designated one of the ''[[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines|Kanpei-taisha]]'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. == Religious significance == The four main ''[[kami]]'' enshrined here are [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]], Himegami, [[Futsunushi no Mikoto|Futsunushi no mikoto]], and [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]].{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods : a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}} Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a [[Syncretism|syncretic,]] combined deity known as Kasuga Daimyōjin, or the "great bright kami of Kasuga."{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|first=Michael|last=Ashkenazi|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} This amalgam lead to the creation of the "Cult of the Kasuga" in which devotees could worship multiple kami at once. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[deity]] and [[Shinto]] ''[[kami]]'' counterpart. The fifth deity, Ame no oshikumone, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]] and Himegami. The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once. == Architecture == The architectural style of Kasuga-taisha comes from the name of it's main hall (''[[honden]]'') known as ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]].'' This style consists of gold and red tones that are reminiscent of Chinese architecture. The shrine complex is protected by four [[cloister]]s and contains a main sanctuary, treasure house, several different halls, and large gates. One beautiful aspect of this shrine is the many wisteria trees known as "''Sunazuri-no-Fuji''" that bloom in late April and early May. This shrine is also home to over 3,000 lanterns which are made of either stone or bronze. An entire hall is devoted to them which is ''Fujinami-no-ya'' Hall but the lanterns are only lit during the [[Setsubun|Setsubun Mantoro]] and [[Bon Festival|Chugen]] Mantoro festivals. The four main [[kami]] each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same [[Kasuga-zukuri|architectural style]]. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, [[katsuogi]] (decorative logs), and [[Chigi (architecture)|chigi]] (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines : a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|first=Joseph|last=Cali|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]], the second to [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi no mikoto]], the third to [[Ame-no-Koyane|Amenokoyane no mikoto]], and the final hall is attributed to the consort, Himegami. Several auxillary shrines lie outside the main sanctuary that are dedicated to lesser [[kami]]. One is alloted to Tsunofuri no kami, that is commonly known as Tsubakimoto Jinja Shrine or Kayabusa Myojin. Kasenomiya Jinja Shrine is atttributed to [[Shinatsuhiko|Shinatsuhiko no mikoto]] and Shinatsuhime who are kami of the winds. Wakamiya Jinja Shrine, created in 1135 CE, is one of the more prominent auxillary shrines because it houses the ''kogami,'' or offspring kami called Ame no Oshikumono no mikoto. The primary worship here revolves around vengeful gods and the dead and is the location of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. The Treasure House at this shrine contains hundreds national treasures as well as about many other cultural properties, most of which are from the [[Heian period]]. Some of the most noteworthy items that reside here are ornate [[Taiko Drum|taiko drums]] used in [[gagaku]] from the [[Kamakura period]], arrows with crystal whistles from the [[Heian period]], and bronze mirrors of the Heian and [[Nanboku-chō period|Nanboku-cho]] periods.{{Cite web|url=https://www.tnm.jp/modules/r_free_page/index.php?id=1814&lang=en|title=Eternal Treasures from Kasugataisha Shrine|last=東京国立博物館 -トーハク-|website=www.tnm.jp|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} ==Festivals== During the festivals of ''[[Setsubun]] Mantoro'' (February 3) and ''Chugen Mantoro'' (August 14–15), three thousand shrine lanterns are all lit at once. The [[Setsubun]] Mantoro refers to the celebration of the seasonal shift from winter to spring while the [[Chugen]] Mantoro relates to the transition of summer to fall. They both takes place in order to celebrate the [[Obon]] and [[Setsubun]] holidays in Japanese culture. At Kasuga Grand shrine, people are seen writing and attaching their wishes, or [[Ema (Shinto)|''ema'']], to the lanterns before lighting them during both festivals. Additionally, it is said that tossing dried beans at these times will ward off bad luck in the future.{{Cite web|url=https://www.japan.travel/en/spot/51/|title=Setsubun Mantoro {{!}} Nara Attractions {{!}} Japan Travel {{!}} JNTO {{!}}|website=Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO)|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} March 13 is the ''Kasuga Matsuri,'' a local festival which features the dances of [[gagaku]] and [[bugaku]]. Shinto women perform traditional Japanese Yamato-mai dances that date back to the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Nara period]]s. This festival also holds a horse celebration which consists of a parade through the streets by a "sacred" horse.{{Cite journal|last=Smyers|first=Karen A.|last2=Bocking|first2=Brian|date=1997|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2385644|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=52|issue=3|pages=419|doi=10.2307/2385644|issn=0027-0741}} One will see people dressed in traditional costumes of the [[Heian period|Heian]] to [[Edo period|Edo]] periods and can experience authentic ''[[kagura]]'' dance displays with ''[[dengaku]]'' music. The Kasuga Wakamiya Festival takes place at the Wakamiya Jinja shrine from December 15 to 18th each year. The main goal of this gathering was to ward off disease while promoting new growth for the spring.{{Cite book|title=Collected writings of P.G. O'Neill = P.G.オニール論文集|last=O'Neill, P. G. |date=2001|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410506|oclc=46594973}} Like ''Kasuga Matsuri'', attendants can see kagura performances along with a procession in traditional attire. ==Kasugayama Primeval Forest== Kasugayama Primeval Forest is [[primeval forest]] of about 250 hectares (620 acres) near the summit of Kasugayama (498 metres (1,634 ft)), and contains 175 kinds of [[trees]], 60 [[bird]] types, and 1,180 species of [[insects]]. In this area adjacent to Kasuga Grand Shrine, hunting and logging have been prohibited since 841 CE. Because Kasugayama has long been tied to Kasuga Grand Shrine worship, it is regarded as a sacred hill. The forest backdrop of the Kasuga Grand Shrine's buildings today has been unchanged since the [[Nara period]].{{dashboard.wikiedu.org student editor|course=[[Wikipedia:Wiki Ed/University of the South/Sacred Arts of Japan (spring)]]|slug=University_of_the_South/Sacred_Arts_of_Japan_(spring)}} ==Images== File:Kasuga-taisha02st3200.jpg|Chakutoden File:Kasuga-taisha01bs3200.jpg|Kurumayadori File:Kasuga-taisha07bs4592.jpg|Minamimon File:Kasuga-taisha26ns3200.jpg|Sakadono File:Kasuga-taisha05n3200.jpg|''[[Heiden (Shinto)|Heiden]]'', Buden File:Kasuga-taisha25n4592.jpg|Keishoden File:Kasuga Shrine inside laterns.jpg|A smaller enclave File:Kasuga-taisha17ns4592.jpg|Lanterns File:Kasuga Grand Shrine.JPG|Corridors in the shrine complex File:Kasuga Shrine lanterns-01.jpg|Lanterns File:Bronze_lanterns,_Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Bronze lanterns File:Kasuga-taisha shrine in Nara 01.jpg|Bronze lanterns in Kasuga-taisha File:03-05-JPN129.jpg|Stone lantern leading up to shrine framing a Nara Park deer File:KasugaTaisha2.jpg|Tying [[Omikuji]] at Kasuga Shrine File:KasugaShrine.JPG|Path leading up to the shrine, braced by rows of stone lanterns File:Canberra_Nara_park.JPG|Kasuga stone lantern presented in 1997 to Nara sister city, [[Canberra, Australian Capital Territory]] File:Kasuga Shrine breast plaques.jpg|A "breast shrine" at the Kasuga Shrine walk decked with [[Ema (Shinto)|Ema]] plaques File:2018 Ichi-no-Torii of Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Ichi-no-[[Torii]] file:Armour red threads Kasuga shrine.jpg|Armour laced with red threads With bamboo, tiger, sparrow motif; nomination includes the helmet; said to have been dedicated by Minamoto no Yoshitsune; one of two similar armours at Kasuga-taisha 1185　Kamakura period Ō-yoroi File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 01.jpg|Hanging lanterns and Andons in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 09.jpg|Hanging lanterns and [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Andon|Andon]]s in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival. Andons, there are special prayers to the reconstruction and welfare for the victims of the [[2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami|Great East Japan earthquake]] and [[Tropical Storm Talas (2011)#Impact|the 2011 flood disaster]]. File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 08.jpg|Hanging lantern designed a drooping wisteria in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival File:Sunazuri-no-Fuji 20140503 01.jpg|"Sunazuri-no-Fuji", [[wisteria]] flowers drooping down to reach the sand on the ground File:Monks in Kasuga-taisha shrine in Nara 06.jpg|Monks in Kasuga-taisha File:Kasuga-taisha shrine in Nara 07.jpg|[[Ema (Shinto)|ema]] (wishes) in asuga-taisha shrine ==See also== {{Portal|Japan|Shinto}} {{Shinto}}[https://www.narahaku.go.jp/english/exhibition/2018toku/kasuga/kasuga_press_list_e.pdf List of National Treasures in Kasuga Treasure House] [http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/main_sanctuary_en.html Map of Kasuga Grand Shrine] [[List of Shinto shrines]] [[Twenty-Two Shrines]] [[List of National Treasures of Japan (crafts-others)]] [[List of National Treasures of Japan (crafts-swords)]] [[List of National Treasures of Japan (shrines)]] [[Deer (mythology)]] [[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines]] [[Kasuga (disambiguation)|Kasuga Maru]] [[List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments]] ==References== {{reflist|33em}} * ==External links== {{commons category|Kasuga-taisha}} * [http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/ Official site in Japanese] * [https://visitnara.jp/venues/A00487/ Kasugataisha Shrine, from The Official Nara Travel Guide] * [https://visitnara.jp/venues/A00487/ Mt. An entire hall is devoted to them which is ''Fujinami-no-ya'' Hall but the lanterns are only lit during the [[Setsubun|Setsubun Mantoro]] and [[Bon Festival|Chugen]] Mantoro festivals. The four main [[kami]] each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same [[Kasuga-zukuri|architectural style]]. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, [[katsuogi]] (decorative logs), and [[Chigi (architecture)|chigi]] (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines : a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|first=Joseph|last=Cali|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]], the second to [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi no mikoto]], the third to [[Ame-no-Koyane|Amenokoyane no mikoto]], and the final hall is attributed to the consort, Himegami. Several auxillary shrines lie outside the main sanctuary that are dedicated to lesser [[kami]]. One is alloted to Tsunofuri no kami, that is commonly known as Tsubakimoto Jinja Shrine or Kayabusa Myojin. Kasenomiya Jinja Shrine is atttributed to [[Shinatsuhiko|Shinatsuhiko no mikoto]] and Shinatsuhime who are kami of the winds. Wakamiya Jinja Shrine, created in 1135 CE, is one of the more prominent auxillary shrines because it houses the ''kogami,'' or offspring kami called Ame no Oshikumono no mikoto. The primary worship here revolves around vengeful gods and the dead and is the location of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. The Treasure House at this shrine contains hundreds national treasures as well as about many other cultural properties, most of which are from the [[Heian period]]. Some of the most noteworthy items that reside here are ornate [[Taiko Drum|taiko drums]] used in [[gagaku]] from the [[Kamakura period]], arrows with crystal whistles from the [[Heian period]], and bronze mirrors of the Heian and [[Nanboku-chō period|Nanboku-cho]] periods.{{Cite web|url=https://www.tnm.jp/modules/r_free_page/index.php?id=1814&lang=en|title=Eternal Treasures from Kasugataisha Shrine|last=東京国立博物館 -トーハク-|website=www.tnm.jp|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} ==Festivals== During the festivals of ''[[Setsubun]] Mantoro'' (February 3) and ''Chugen Mantoro'' (August 14–15), three thousand shrine lanterns are all lit at once. The [[Setsubun]] Mantoro refers to the celebration of the seasonal shift from winter to spring while the [[Chugen]] Mantoro relates to the transition of summer to fall. They both takes place in order to celebrate the [[Obon]] and [[Setsubun]] holidays in Japanese culture. At Kasuga Grand shrine, people are seen writing and attaching their wishes, or [[Ema (Shinto)|''ema'']], to the lanterns before lighting them during both festivals. Additionally, it is said that tossing dried beans at these times will ward off bad luck in the future.{{Cite web|url=https://www.japan.travel/en/spot/51/|title=Setsubun Mantoro {{!}} Nara Attractions {{!}} Japan Travel {{!}} JNTO {{!}}|website=Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO)|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} March 13 is the ''Kasuga Matsuri,'' a local festival which features the dances of [[gagaku]] and [[bugaku]]. Shinto women perform traditional Japanese Yamato-mai dances that date back to the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Nara period]]s. This festival also holds a horse celebration which consists of a parade through the streets by a "sacred" horse.{{Cite journal|last=Smyers|first=Karen A.|last2=Bocking|first2=Brian|date=1997|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2385644|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=52|issue=3|pages=419|doi=10.2307/2385644|issn=0027-0741}} One will see people dressed in traditional costumes of the [[Heian period|Heian]] to [[Edo period|Edo]] periods and can experience authentic ''[[kagura]]'' dance displays with ''[[dengaku]]'' music. The Kasuga Wakamiya Festival takes place at the Wakamiya Jinja shrine from December 15 to 18th each year. The main goal of this gathering was to ward off disease while promoting new growth for the spring.{{Cite book|title=Collected writings of P.G. O'Neill = P.G.オニール論文集|last=O'Neill, P. G. |date=2001|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410506|oclc=46594973}} Like ''Kasuga Matsuri'', attendants can see kagura performances along with a procession in traditional attire. ==Kasugayama Primeval Forest== Kasugayama Primeval Forest is [[primeval forest]] of about 250 hectares (620 acres) near the summit of Kasugayama (498 metres (1,634 ft)), and contains 175 kinds of [[trees]], 60 [[bird]] types, and 1,180 species of [[insects]]. In this area adjacent to Kasuga Grand Shrine, hunting and logging have been prohibited since 841 CE. Because Kasugayama has long been tied to Kasuga Grand Shrine worship, it is regarded as a sacred hill. The forest backdrop of the Kasuga Grand Shrine's buildings today has been unchanged since the [[Nara period]].{{dashboard.wikiedu.org student editor|course=[[Wikipedia:Wiki Ed/University of the South/Sacred Arts of Japan (spring)]]|slug=University_of_the_South/Sacred_Arts_of_Japan_(spring)}} ==Images== File:Kasuga-taisha02st3200.jpg|Chakutoden File:Kasuga-taisha01bs3200.jpg|Kurumayadori File:Kasuga-taisha07bs4592.jpg|Minamimon File:Kasuga-taisha26ns3200.jpg|Sakadono File:Kasuga-taisha05n3200.jpg|''[[Heiden (Shinto)|Heiden]]'', Buden File:Kasuga-taisha25n4592.jpg|Keishoden File:Kasuga Shrine inside laterns.jpg|A smaller enclave File:Kasuga-taisha17ns4592.jpg|Lanterns File:Kasuga Grand Shrine.JPG|Corridors in the shrine complex File:Kasuga Shrine lanterns-01.jpg|Lanterns File:Bronze_lanterns,_Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Bronze lanterns File:Kasuga-taisha shrine in Nara 01.jpg|Bronze lanterns in Kasuga-taisha File:03-05-JPN129.jpg|Stone lantern leading up to shrine framing a Nara Park deer File:KasugaTaisha2.jpg|Tying [[Omikuji]] at Kasuga Shrine File:KasugaShrine.JPG|Path leading up to the shrine, braced by rows of stone lanterns File:Canberra_Nara_park.JPG|Kasuga stone lantern presented in 1997 to Nara sister city, [[Canberra, Australian Capital Territory]] File:Kasuga Shrine breast plaques.jpg|A "breast shrine" at the Kasuga Shrine walk decked with [[Ema (Shinto)|Ema]] plaques File:2018 Ichi-no-Torii of Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Ichi-no-[[Torii]] file:Armour red threads Kasuga shrine.jpg|Armour laced with red threads With bamboo, tiger, sparrow motif; nomination includes the helmet; said to have been dedicated by Minamoto no Yoshitsune; one of two similar armours at Kasuga-taisha 1185　Kamakura period Ō-yoroi File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 01.jpg|Hanging lanterns and Andons in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 09.jpg|Hanging lanterns and [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Andon|Andon]]s in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival. (Kasuga-sai: 春日祭) (13th March) | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Kasuga Grand Shrine'''|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Nara, Nara|Nara]], [[Nara prefecture|Nara Prefecture]], [[Japan]].Richard, Ponsonby-Fane. (1964) '' Visiting Famous Shrines in Japan,'' pp. 221-251. Established in 768 CE and rebuilt several times over the centuries, it is the shrine of the [[Fujiwara family]]. The interior is famous for its many bronze lanterns, as well as the many [[Tōrō|stone lantern]]s that lead up the shrine. The architectural style ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]]'' takes its name from Kasuga Shrine's ''[[honden]]'' (sanctuary). Kasuga Shrine, and the '''Kasugayama Primeval Forest''' near it, are registered as a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] as part of the "[[Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara]]". The path to Kasuga Shrine passes through a deer park. In the deer park, deer are able to roam freely and are believed to be sacred messengers of the Shinto gods that inhabit the shrine and surrounding mountainous terrain. Kasuga Shrine and the deer have been featured in several paintings and works of art of the [[Nambokucho Period]].{{cite book|last=[[Birmingham Museum of Art]]|title=Birmingham Museum of Art : guide to the collection|year=2010|publisher=Birmingham Museum of Art|location=[Birmingham, Ala]|isbn=978-1-904832-77-5|pages=46|url=http://artsbma.org}} Over three thousand stone lanterns line the way. The [[Manyo Botanical Garden, Nara|Man'yo Botanical Garden, Nara]] is adjacent to the shrine. == History == === Origin === The birth of this shrine, according to legend, began when the first kami of Kasuga-taisha, [[Takemikazuchi]], rode on the back of a white deer to the top of [[Mount Wakakusa|Mount Mikasa]] in 768 CE.{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|first=Royall|last=Tyler|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} This kami is said to have traveled from the [[Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingu Shrine]] in order to protect [[Nara]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|title=Main Sanctuary|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} The shrine location first received favor from the Imperial government in the [[Heian period]] as a result of the power from the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara family]] as well as [[Empress Shotoku]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/index.html|title=世界遺産 春日大社 公式ホームページ|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} From 1871 through 1946, Kasuga Shrine was officially designated one of the ''[[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines|Kanpei-taisha]]'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. == Religious significance == The four main ''[[kami]]'' enshrined here are [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]], Himegami, [[Futsunushi no Mikoto|Futsunushi no mikoto]], and [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]].{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods : a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}} Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a [[Syncretism|syncretic,]] combined deity known as Kasuga Daimyōjin, or the "great bright kami of Kasuga."{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|first=Michael|last=Ashkenazi|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} This amalgam lead to the creation of the "Cult of the Kasuga" in which devotees could worship multiple kami at once. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[deity]] and [[Shinto]] ''[[kami]]'' counterpart. The fifth deity, Ame no oshikumone, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]] and Himegami. (1964) '' Visiting Famous Shrines in Japan,'' pp. 221-251. Established in 768 CE and rebuilt several times over the centuries, it is the shrine of the [[Fujiwara family]]. The interior is famous for its many bronze lanterns, as well as the many [[Tōrō|stone lantern]]s that lead up the shrine. The architectural style ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]]'' takes its name from Kasuga Shrine's ''[[honden]]'' (sanctuary). Kasuga Shrine, and the '''Kasugayama Primeval Forest''' near it, are registered as a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] as part of the "[[Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara]]". The path to Kasuga Shrine passes through a deer park. In the deer park, deer are able to roam freely and are believed to be sacred messengers of the Shinto gods that inhabit the shrine and surrounding mountainous terrain. Kasuga Shrine and the deer have been featured in several paintings and works of art of the [[Nambokucho Period]].{{cite book|last=[[Birmingham Museum of Art]]|title=Birmingham Museum of Art : guide to the collection|year=2010|publisher=Birmingham Museum of Art|location=[Birmingham, Ala]|isbn=978-1-904832-77-5|pages=46|url=http://artsbma.org}} Over three thousand stone lanterns line the way. The [[Manyo Botanical Garden, Nara|Man'yo Botanical Garden, Nara]] is adjacent to the shrine. == History == === Origin === The birth of this shrine, according to legend, began when the first kami of Kasuga-taisha, [[Takemikazuchi]], rode on the back of a white deer to the top of [[Mount Wakakusa|Mount Mikasa]] in 768 CE.{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|first=Royall|last=Tyler|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} This kami is said to have traveled from the [[Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingu Shrine]] in order to protect [[Nara]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|title=Main Sanctuary|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} The shrine location first received favor from the Imperial government in the [[Heian period]] as a result of the power from the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara family]] as well as [[Empress Shotoku]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/index.html|title=世界遺産 春日大社 公式ホームページ|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} From 1871 through 1946, Kasuga Shrine was officially designated one of the ''[[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines|Kanpei-taisha]]'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. == Religious significance == The four main ''[[kami]]'' enshrined here are [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]], Himegami, [[Futsunushi no Mikoto|Futsunushi no mikoto]], and [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]].{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods : a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}} Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a [[Syncretism|syncretic,]] combined deity known as Kasuga Daimyōjin, or the "great bright kami of Kasuga."{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|first=Michael|last=Ashkenazi|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} This amalgam lead to the creation of the "Cult of the Kasuga" in which devotees could worship multiple kami at once. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[deity]] and [[Shinto]] ''[[kami]]'' counterpart. The fifth deity, Ame no oshikumone, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]] and Himegami. The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once. == Architecture == The architectural style of Kasuga-taisha comes from the name of it's main hall (''[[honden]]'') known as ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]].'' This style consists of gold and red tones that are reminiscent of Chinese architecture. The shrine complex is protected by four [[cloister]]s and contains a main sanctuary, treasure house, several different halls, and large gates. One beautiful aspect of this shrine is the many wisteria trees known as "''Sunazuri-no-Fuji''" that bloom in late April and early May. This shrine is also home to over 3,000 lanterns which are made of either stone or bronze. An entire hall is devoted to them which is ''Fujinami-no-ya'' Hall but the lanterns are only lit during the [[Setsubun|Setsubun Mantoro]] and [[Bon Festival|Chugen]] Mantoro festivals. The four main [[kami]] each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same [[Kasuga-zukuri|architectural style]]. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, [[katsuogi]] (decorative logs), and [[Chigi (architecture)|chigi]] (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines : a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|first=Joseph|last=Cali|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]], the second to [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi no mikoto]], the third to [[Ame-no-Koyane|Amenokoyane no mikoto]], and the final hall is attributed to the consort, Himegami. Several auxillary shrines lie outside the main sanctuary that are dedicated to lesser [[kami]]. One is alloted to Tsunofuri no kami, that is commonly known as Tsubakimoto Jinja Shrine or Kayabusa Myojin. Kasenomiya Jinja Shrine is atttributed to [[Shinatsuhiko|Shinatsuhiko no mikoto]] and Shinatsuhime who are kami of the winds. Wakamiya Jinja Shrine, created in 1135 CE, is one of the more prominent auxillary shrines because it houses the ''kogami,'' or offspring kami called Ame no Oshikumono no mikoto. The primary worship here revolves around vengeful gods and the dead and is the location of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. The Treasure House at this shrine contains hundreds national treasures as well as about many other cultural properties, most of which are from the [[Heian period]]. Some of the most noteworthy items that reside here are ornate [[Taiko Drum|taiko drums]] used in [[gagaku]] from the [[Kamakura period]], arrows with crystal whistles from the [[Heian period]], and bronze mirrors of the Heian and [[Nanboku-chō period|Nanboku-cho]] periods.{{Cite web|url=https://www.tnm.jp/modules/r_free_page/index.php?id=1814&lang=en|title=Eternal Treasures from Kasugataisha Shrine|last=東京国立博物館 -トーハク-|website=www.tnm.jp|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} ==Festivals== During the festivals of ''[[Setsubun]] Mantoro'' (February 3) and ''Chugen Mantoro'' (August 14–15), three thousand shrine lanterns are all lit at once. The [[Setsubun]] Mantoro refers to the celebration of the seasonal shift from winter to spring while the [[Chugen]] Mantoro relates to the transition of summer to fall. They both takes place in order to celebrate the [[Obon]] and [[Setsubun]] holidays in Japanese culture. At Kasuga Grand shrine, people are seen writing and attaching their wishes, or [[Ema (Shinto)|''ema'']], to the lanterns before lighting them during both festivals. Additionally, it is said that tossing dried beans at these times will ward off bad luck in the future.{{Cite web|url=https://www.japan.travel/en/spot/51/|title=Setsubun Mantoro {{!}} Nara Attractions {{!}} Japan Travel {{!}} JNTO {{!}}|website=Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO)|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} March 13 is the ''Kasuga Matsuri,'' a local festival which features the dances of [[gagaku]] and [[bugaku]]. Shinto women perform traditional Japanese Yamato-mai dances that date back to the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Nara period]]s. This festival also holds a horse celebration which consists of a parade through the streets by a "sacred" horse.{{Cite journal|last=Smyers|first=Karen A.|last2=Bocking|first2=Brian|date=1997|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2385644|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=52|issue=3|pages=419|doi=10.2307/2385644|issn=0027-0741}} One will see people dressed in traditional costumes of the [[Heian period|Heian]] to [[Edo period|Edo]] periods and can experience authentic ''[[kagura]]'' dance displays with ''[[dengaku]]'' music. The Kasuga Wakamiya Festival takes place at the Wakamiya Jinja shrine from December 15 to 18th each year. The main goal of this gathering was to ward off disease while promoting new growth for the spring.{{Cite book|title=Collected writings of P.G. O'Neill = P.G.オニール論文集|last=O'Neill, P. G. |date=2001|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410506|oclc=46594973}} Like ''Kasuga Matsuri'', attendants can see kagura performances along with a procession in traditional attire. ==Kasugayama Primeval Forest== Kasugayama Primeval Forest is [[primeval forest]] of about 250 hectares (620 acres) near the summit of Kasugayama (498 metres (1,634 ft)), and contains 175 kinds of [[trees]], 60 [[bird]] types, and 1,180 species of [[insects]]. In this area adjacent to Kasuga Grand Shrine, hunting and logging have been prohibited since 841 CE. Because Kasugayama has long been tied to Kasuga Grand Shrine worship, it is regarded as a sacred hill. The forest backdrop of the Kasuga Grand Shrine's buildings today has been unchanged since the [[Nara period]].{{dashboard.wikiedu.org student editor|course=[[Wikipedia:Wiki Ed/University of the South/Sacred Arts of Japan (spring)]]|slug=University_of_the_South/Sacred_Arts_of_Japan_(spring)}} ==Images== File:Kasuga-taisha02st3200.jpg|Chakutoden File:Kasuga-taisha01bs3200.jpg|Kurumayadori File:Kasuga-taisha07bs4592.jpg|Minamimon File:Kasuga-taisha26ns3200.jpg|Sakadono File:Kasuga-taisha05n3200.jpg|''[[Heiden (Shinto)|Heiden]]'', Buden File:Kasuga-taisha25n4592.jpg|Keishoden File:Kasuga Shrine inside laterns.jpg|A smaller enclave File:Kasuga-taisha17ns4592.jpg|Lanterns File:Kasuga Grand Shrine.JPG|Corridors in the shrine complex File:Kasuga Shrine lanterns-01.jpg|Lanterns File:Bronze_lanterns,_Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Bronze lanterns File:Kasuga-taisha shrine in Nara 01.jpg|Bronze lanterns in Kasuga-taisha File:03-05-JPN129.jpg|Stone lantern leading up to shrine framing a Nara Park deer File:KasugaTaisha2.jpg|Tying [[Omikuji]] at Kasuga Shrine File:KasugaShrine.JPG|Path leading up to the shrine, braced by rows of stone lanterns File:Canberra_Nara_park.JPG|Kasuga stone lantern presented in 1997 to Nara sister city, [[Canberra, Australian Capital Territory]] File:Kasuga Shrine breast plaques.jpg|A "breast shrine" at the Kasuga Shrine walk decked with [[Ema (Shinto)|Ema]] plaques File:2018 Ichi-no-Torii of Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Ichi-no-[[Torii]] file:Armour red threads Kasuga shrine.jpg|Armour laced with red threads With bamboo, tiger, sparrow motif; nomination includes the helmet; said to have been dedicated by Minamoto no Yoshitsune; one of two similar armours at Kasuga-taisha 1185　Kamakura period Ō-yoroi File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 01.jpg|Hanging lanterns and Andons in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 09.jpg|Hanging lanterns and [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Andon|Andon]]s in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival. Andons, there are special prayers to the reconstruction and welfare for the victims of the [[2011 Tōhoku earthquake and tsunami|Great East Japan earthquake]] and [[Tropical Storm Talas (2011)#Impact|the 2011 flood disaster]]. (Kasuga-sai: 春日祭) (13th March) | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Kasuga Grand Shrine'''|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Nara, Nara|Nara]], [[Nara Prefecture]], [[Japan]].Richard, Ponsonby-Fane. (1964) '' Visiting Famous Shrines in Japan,'' pp. 221-251. Established in 768 CE and rebuilt several times over the centuries, it is the shrine of the [[Fujiwara family]]. The interior is famous for its many bronze lanterns, as well as the many [[Tōrō|stone lantern]]s that lead up the shrine. The architectural style ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]]'' takes its name from Kasuga Shrine's ''[[honden]]'' (sanctuary). Kasuga Shrine, and the '''Kasugayama Primeval Forest''' near it, are registered as a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] as part of the "[[Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara]]". The path to Kasuga Shrine passes through a deer park. In the deer park, deer are able to roam freely and are believed to be sacred messengers of the Shinto gods that inhabit the shrine and surrounding mountainous terrain. Kasuga Shrine and the deer have been featured in several paintings and works of art of the [[Nambokucho Period]].{{cite book|last=[[Birmingham Museum of Art]]|title=Birmingham Museum of Art : guide to the collection|year=2010|publisher=Birmingham Museum of Art|location=[Birmingham, Ala]|isbn=978-1-904832-77-5|pages=46|url=http://artsbma.org}} Over three thousand stone lanterns line the way. The [[Manyo Botanical Garden, Nara|Man'yo Botanical Garden]] is adjacent to the shrine. == History == === Origin === The birth of this shrine, according to legend, began when the first kami of Kasuga-taisha, [[Takemikazuchi]], rode on the back of a white deer to the top of [[Mount Wakakusa|Mount Mikasa]] in 768 CE.{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|first=Royall|last=Tyler|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} This kami is said to have traveled from the [[Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingu Shrine]] in order to protect [[Nara]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|title=Main Sanctuary|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} The shrine location first received favor from the Imperial government in the [[Heian period]] as a result of the power from the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara family]] as well as [[Empress Shotoku]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/index.html|title=世界遺産 春日大社 公式ホームページ|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} From 1871 through 1946, Kasuga Shrine was officially designated one of the ''[[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines|Kanpei-taisha]]'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. == Religious significance == The four main ''[[kami]]'' enshrined here are [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]], Himegami, [[Futsunushi no Mikoto|Futsunushi no mikoto]], and [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]].{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods : a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}} Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a [[Syncretism|syncretic,]] combined deity known as Kasuga Daimyōjin, or the "great bright kami of Kasuga."{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|first=Michael|last=Ashkenazi|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} This amalgam lead to the creation of the "Cult of the Kasuga" in which devotees could worship multiple kami at once. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[deity]] and [[Shinto]] ''[[kami]]'' counterpart. The fifth deity, Ame no oshikumone, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]] and Himegami. The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once. == Architecture == The architectural style of Kasuga-taisha comes from the name of it's main hall (''[[honden]]'') known as ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]].'' This style consists of gold and red tones that are reminiscent of Chinese architecture. The shrine complex is protected by four [[cloister]]s and contains a main sanctuary, treasure house, several different halls, and large gates. One beautiful aspect of this shrine is the many wisteria trees known as "''Sunazuri-no-Fuji''" that bloom in late April and early May. This shrine is also home to over 3,000 lanterns which are made of either stone or bronze. An entire hall is devoted to them which is ''Fujinami-no-ya'' Hall but the lanterns are only lit during the [[Setsubun|Setsubun Mantoro]] and [[Bon Festival|Chugen]] Mantoro festivals. The four main [[kami]] each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same [[Kasuga-zukuri|architectural style]]. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, [[katsuogi]] (decorative logs), and [[Chigi (architecture)|chigi]] (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines : a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|first=Joseph|last=Cali|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]], the second to [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi no mikoto]], the third to [[Ame-no-Koyane|Amenokoyane no mikoto]], and the final hall is attributed to the consort, Himegami. Several auxillary shrines lie outside the main sanctuary that are dedicated to lesser [[kami]]. One is alloted to Tsunofuri no kami, that is commonly known as Tsubakimoto Jinja Shrine or Kayabusa Myojin. Kasenomiya Jinja Shrine is atttributed to [[Shinatsuhiko|Shinatsuhiko no mikoto]] and Shinatsuhime who are kami of the winds. Wakamiya Jinja Shrine, created in 1135 CE, is one of the more prominent auxillary shrines because it houses the ''kogami,'' or offspring kami called Ame no Oshikumono no mikoto. The primary worship here revolves around vengeful gods and the dead and is the location of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. The Treasure House at this shrine contains hundreds national treasures as well as about many other cultural properties, most of which are from the [[Heian period]]. Some of the most noteworthy items that reside here are ornate [[Taiko Drum|taiko drums]] used in [[gagaku]] from the [[Kamakura period]], arrows with crystal whistles from the [[Heian period]], and bronze mirrors of the Heian and [[Nanboku-chō period|Nanboku-cho]] periods.{{Cite web|url=https://www.tnm.jp/modules/r_free_page/index.php?id=1814&lang=en|title=Eternal Treasures from Kasugataisha Shrine|last=東京国立博物館 -トーハク-|website=www.tnm.jp|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} ==Festivals== During the festivals of ''[[Setsubun]] Mantoro'' (February 3) and ''Chugen Mantoro'' (August 14–15), three thousand shrine lanterns are all lit at once. The [[Setsubun]] Mantoro refers to the celebration of the seasonal shift from winter to spring while the [[Chugen]] Mantoro relates to the transition of summer to fall. They both takes place in order to celebrate the [[Obon]] and [[Setsubun]] holidays in Japanese culture. At Kasuga Grand shrine, people are seen writing and attaching their wishes, or [[Ema (Shinto)|''ema'']], to the lanterns before lighting them during both festivals. Additionally, it is said that tossing dried beans at these times will ward off bad luck in the future.{{Cite web|url=https://www.japan.travel/en/spot/51/|title=Setsubun Mantoro {{!}} Nara Attractions {{!}} Japan Travel {{!}} JNTO {{!}}|website=Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO)|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} March 13 is the ''Kasuga Matsuri,'' a local festival which features the dances of [[gagaku]] and [[bugaku]]. Shinto women perform traditional Japanese Yamato-mai dances that date back to the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Nara period]]s. This festival also holds a horse celebration which consists of a parade through the streets by a "sacred" horse.{{Cite journal|last=Smyers|first=Karen A.|last2=Bocking|first2=Brian|date=1997|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2385644|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=52|issue=3|pages=419|doi=10.2307/2385644|issn=0027-0741}} One will see people dressed in traditional costumes of the [[Heian period|Heian]] to [[Edo period|Edo]] periods and can experience authentic ''[[kagura]]'' dance displays with ''[[dengaku]]'' music. The Kasuga Wakamiya Festival takes place at the Wakamiya Jinja shrine from December 15 to 18th each year. The main goal of this gathering was to ward off disease while promoting new growth for the spring.{{Cite book|title=Collected writings of P.G. O'Neill = P.G.オニール論文集|last=O'Neill, P. G. |date=2001|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410506|oclc=46594973}} Like ''Kasuga Matsuri'', attendants can see kagura performances along with a procession in traditional attire. ==Kasugayama Primeval Forest== Kasugayama Primeval Forest is [[primeval forest]] of about 250 hectares (620 acres) near the summit of Kasugayama (498 metres (1,634 ft)), and contains 175 kinds of [[trees]], 60 [[bird]] types, and 1,180 species of [[insects]]. In this area adjacent to Kasuga Grand Shrine, hunting and logging have been prohibited since 841 CE. Because Kasugayama has long been tied to Kasuga Grand Shrine worship, it is regarded as a sacred hill. The forest backdrop of the Kasuga Grand Shrine's buildings today has been unchanged since the [[Nara period]].{{dashboard.wikiedu.org student editor|course=[[Wikipedia:Wiki Ed/University of the South/Sacred Arts of Japan ==Images== File:Kasuga-taisha02st3200.jpg|Chakutoden File:Kasuga-taisha01bs3200.jpg|Kurumayadori File:Kasuga-taisha07bs4592.jpg|Minamimon File:Kasuga-taisha26ns3200.jpg|Sakadono File:Kasuga-taisha05n3200.jpg|''[[Heiden (Shinto)|Heiden]]'', Buden File:Kasuga-taisha25n4592.jpg|Keishoden File:Kasuga Shrine inside laterns.jpg|A smaller enclave File:Kasuga-taisha17ns4592.jpg|Lanterns File:Kasuga Grand Shrine.JPG|Corridors in the shrine complex File:Kasuga Shrine lanterns-01.jpg|Lanterns File:Bronze_lanterns,_Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Bronze lanterns File:Kasuga-taisha shrine in Nara 01.jpg|Bronze lanterns in Kasuga-taisha File:03-05-JPN129.jpg|Stone lantern leading up to shrine framing a Nara Park deer File:KasugaTaisha2.jpg|Tying [[Omikuji]] at Kasuga Shrine File:KasugaShrine.JPG|Path leading up to the shrine, braced by rows of stone lanterns File:Canberra_Nara_park.JPG|Kasuga stone lantern presented in 1997 to Nara sister city, [[Canberra, Australian Capital Territory]] File:Kasuga Shrine breast plaques.jpg|A "breast shrine" at the Kasuga Shrine walk decked with [[Ema (Shinto)|Ema]] plaques File:2018 Ichi-no-Torii of Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Ichi-no-[[Torii]] file:Armour red threads Kasuga shrine.jpg|Armour laced with red threads With bamboo, tiger, sparrow motif; nomination includes the helmet; said to have been dedicated by Minamoto no Yoshitsune; one of two similar armours at Kasuga-taisha 1185　Kamakura period Ō-yoroi File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 01.jpg|Hanging lanterns and Andons in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 09.jpg|Hanging lanterns and [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Andon|Andon]]s in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, [[katsuogi]] (decorative logs), and [[Chigi (architecture)|chigi]] (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines : a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|first=Joseph|last=Cali|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]], the second to [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi no mikoto]], the third to [[Ame-no-Koyane|Amenokoyane no mikoto]], and the final hall is attributed to the consort, Himegami. Several auxillary shrines lie outside the main sanctuary that are dedicated to lesser [[kami]]. One is alloted to Tsunofuri no kami, that is commonly known as Tsubakimoto Jinja Shrine or Kayabusa Myojin. Kasenomiya Jinja Shrine is atttributed to [[Shinatsuhiko|Shinatsuhiko no mikoto]] and Shinatsuhime who are kami of the winds. Wakamiya Jinja Shrine, created in 1135 CE, is one of the more prominent auxillary shrines because it houses the ''kogami,'' or offspring kami called Ame no Oshikumono no mikoto. The primary worship here revolves around vengeful gods and the dead and is the location of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. The Treasure House at this shrine contains hundreds national treasures as well as about many other cultural properties, most of which are from the [[Heian period]]. Some of the most noteworthy items that reside here are ornate [[Taiko Drum|taiko drums]] used in [[gagaku]] from the [[Kamakura period]], arrows with crystal whistles from the [[Heian period]], and bronze mirrors of the Heian and [[Nanboku-chō period|Nanboku-cho]] periods.{{Cite web|url=https://www.tnm.jp/modules/r_free_page/index.php?id=1814&lang=en|title=Eternal Treasures from Kasugataisha Shrine|last=東京国立博物館 -トーハク-|website=www.tnm.jp|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} ==Festivals== During the festivals of ''[[Setsubun]] Mantoro'' (February 3) and ''Chugen Mantoro'' (August 14–15), three thousand shrine lanterns are all lit at once. The [[Setsubun]] Mantoro refers to the celebration of the seasonal shift from winter to spring while the [[Chugen]] Mantoro relates to the transition of summer to fall. They both takes place in order to celebrate the [[Obon]] and [[Setsubun]] holidays in Japanese culture. At Kasuga Grand shrine, people are seen writing and attaching their wishes, or [[Ema (Shinto)|''ema'']], to the lanterns before lighting them during both festivals. Additionally, it is said that tossing dried beans at these times will ward off bad luck in the future.{{Cite web|url=https://www.japan.travel/en/spot/51/|title=Setsubun Mantoro {{!}} Nara Attractions {{!}} Japan Travel {{!}} JNTO {{!}}|website=Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO)|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} March 13 is the ''Kasuga Matsuri,'' a local festival which features the dances of [[gagaku]] and [[bugaku]]. The main goal of this gathering was to ward off disease while promoting new growth for the spring.{{Cite book|title=Collected writings of P.G. O'Neill = P.G.オニール論文集|last=O'Neill, P. G. |date=2001|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410506|oclc=46594973}} Like ''Kasuga Matsuri'', attendants can see kagura performances along with a procession in traditional attire. ==Kasugayama Primeval Forest== Kasugayama Primeval Forest is [[primeval forest]] of about 250 hectares (620 acres) near the summit of Kasugayama (498 metres (1,634 ft)), and contains 175 kinds of [[trees]], 60 [[bird]] types, and 1,180 species of [[insects]]. (1964) '' Visiting Famous Shrines in Japan,'' pp. 221-251. Established in 768 CE and rebuilt several times over the centuries, it is the shrine of the [[Fujiwara family]]. The interior is famous for its many bronze lanterns, as well as the many [[Tōrō|stone lantern]]s that lead up the shrine. The architectural style ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]]'' takes its name from Kasuga Shrine's ''[[honden]]'' (sanctuary). Kasuga Shrine, and the '''Kasugayama Primeval Forest''' near it, are registered as a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] as part of the "[[Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara]]". The path to Kasuga Shrine passes through a deer park. In the deer park, deer are able to roam freely and are believed to be sacred messengers of the Shinto gods that inhabit the shrine and surrounding mountainous terrain. Kasuga Shrine and the deer have been featured in several paintings and works of art of the [[Nambokucho Period]].{{cite book|last=[[Birmingham Museum of Art]]|title=Birmingham Museum of Art : guide to the collection|year=2010|publisher=Birmingham Museum of Art|location=[Birmingham, Ala]|isbn=978-1-904832-77-5|pages=46|url=http://artsbma.org}} Over three thousand stone lanterns line the way. The [[Manyo Botanical Garden, Nara|Man'yo Botanical Garden]] is adjacent to the shrine. == History == === Origin === The birth of this shrine, according to legend, began when the first kami of Kasuga-taisha, [[Takemikazuchi]], rode on the back of a white deer to the top of [[Mount Wakakusa|Mount Mikasa]] in 768 CE.{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|first=Royall|last=Tyler|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} This kami is said to have traveled from the [[Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingu Shrine]] in order to protect [[Nara]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|title=Main Sanctuary|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} The shrine location first received favor from the Imperial government in the [[Heian period]] as a result of the power from the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara family]] as well as [[Empress Shotoku]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/index.html|title=世界遺産 春日大社 公式ホームページ|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} From 1871 through 1946, Kasuga Shrine was officially designated one of the ''[[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines|Kanpei-taisha]]'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. == Religious significance == The four main ''[[kami]]'' enshrined here are [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]], Himegami, [[Futsunushi no Mikoto|Futsunushi no mikoto]], and [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]].{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods : a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}} Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a [[Syncretism|syncretic,]] combined deity known as Kasuga Daimyōjin, or the "great bright kami of Kasuga."{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|first=Michael|last=Ashkenazi|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} This amalgam lead to the creation of the "Cult of the Kasuga" in which devotees could worship multiple kami at once. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[deity]] and [[Shinto]] ''[[kami]]'' counterpart. The [[Manyo Botanical Garden, Nara|Man'yo Botanical Garden]] is adjacent to the shrine. == History == === Origin === The birth of this shrine, according to legend, began when the first kami of Kasuga-taisha, [[Takemikazuchi]], rode on the back of a white deer to the top of [[Mount Wakakusa|Mount Mikasa]] in 768 CE.{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|first=Royall|last=Tyler|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} This kami is said to have traveled from the [[Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingu Shrine]] in order to protect [[Nara]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|title=Main Sanctuary|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} The shrine location first received favor from the Imperial government in the [[Heian period]] as a result of the power from the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara family]] as well as [[Empress Shotoku]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/index.html|title=世界遺産 春日大社 公式ホームページ|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} From 1871 through 1946, Kasuga Shrine was officially designated one of the ''[[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines|Kanpei-taisha]]'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. == Religious significance == The four main ''[[kami]]'' enshrined here are [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]], Himegami, [[Futsunushi no Mikoto|Futsunushi no mikoto]], and [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]].{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods : a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}} Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a [[Syncretism|syncretic,]] combined deity known as Kasuga Daimyōjin, or the "great bright kami of Kasuga."{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|first=Michael|last=Ashkenazi|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} This amalgam lead to the creation of the "Cult of the Kasuga" in which devotees could worship multiple kami at once. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[deity]] and [[Shinto]] ''[[kami]]'' counterpart. The fifth deity, Ame no oshikumone, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]] and Himegami. The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once. == Architecture == The architectural style of Kasuga-taisha comes from the name of it's main hall (''[[honden]]'') known as ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]].'' This style consists of gold and red tones that are reminiscent of Chinese architecture. The shrine complex is protected by four [[cloister]]s and contains a main sanctuary, treasure house, several different halls, and large gates. One beautiful aspect of this shrine is the many wisteria trees known as "''Sunazuri-no-Fuji''" that bloom in late April and early May. This shrine is also home to over 3,000 lanterns which are made of either stone or bronze. An entire hall is devoted to them which is ''Fujinami-no-ya'' Hall but the lanterns are only lit during the [[Setsubun|Setsubun Mantoro]] and [[Bon Festival|Chugen]] Mantoro festivals. The four main [[kami]] each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same [[Kasuga-zukuri|architectural style]]. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, [[katsuogi]] (decorative logs), and [[Chigi (architecture)|chigi]] (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines : a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|first=Joseph|last=Cali|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]], the second to [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi no mikoto]], the third to [[Ame-no-Koyane|Amenokoyane no mikoto]], and the final hall is attributed to the consort, Himegami. Several auxillary shrines lie outside the main sanctuary that are dedicated to lesser [[kami]]. One is alloted to Tsunofuri no kami, that is commonly known as Tsubakimoto Jinja Shrine or Kayabusa Myojin. Kasenomiya Jinja Shrine is atttributed to [[Shinatsuhiko|Shinatsuhiko no mikoto]] and Shinatsuhime who are kami of the winds. Wakamiya Jinja Shrine, created in 1135 CE, is one of the more prominent auxillary shrines because it houses the ''kogami,'' or offspring kami called Ame no Oshikumono no mikoto. The primary worship here revolves around vengeful gods and the dead and is the location of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. The Treasure House at this shrine contains hundreds national treasures as well as about many other cultural properties, most of which are from the [[Heian period]]. Some of the most noteworthy items that reside here are ornate [[Taiko Drum|taiko drums]] used in [[gagaku]] from the [[Kamakura period]], arrows with crystal whistles from the [[Heian period]], and bronze mirrors of the Heian and [[Nanboku-chō period|Nanboku-cho]] periods.{{Cite web|url=https://www.tnm.jp/modules/r_free_page/index.php?id=1814&lang=en|title=Eternal Treasures from Kasugataisha Shrine|last=東京国立博物館 -トーハク-|website=www.tnm.jp|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} ==Festivals== During the festivals of ''[[Setsubun]] Mantoro'' (February 3) and ''Chugen Mantoro'' (August 14–15), three thousand shrine lanterns are all lit at once. The [[Setsubun]] Mantoro refers to the celebration of the seasonal shift from winter to spring while the [[Chugen]] Mantoro relates to the transition of summer to fall. They both takes place in order to celebrate the [[Obon]] and [[Setsubun]] holidays in Japanese culture. At Kasuga Grand shrine, people are seen writing and attaching their wishes, or [[Ema (Shinto)|''ema'']], to the lanterns before lighting them during both festivals. Additionally, it is said that tossing dried beans at these times will ward off bad luck in the future.{{Cite web|url=https://www.japan.travel/en/spot/51/|title=Setsubun Mantoro {{!}} Nara Attractions {{!}} Japan Travel {{!}} JNTO {{!}}|website=Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO)|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} March 13 is the ''Kasuga Matsuri,'' a local festival which features the dances of [[gagaku]] and [[bugaku]]. Shinto women perform traditional Japanese Yamato-mai dances that date back to the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Nara period]]s. This festival also holds a horse celebration which consists of a parade through the streets by a "sacred" horse.{{Cite journal|last=Smyers|first=Karen A.|last2=Bocking|first2=Brian|date=1997|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2385644|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=52|issue=3|pages=419|doi=10.2307/2385644|issn=0027-0741}} One will see people dressed in traditional costumes of the [[Heian period|Heian]] to [[Edo period|Edo]] periods and can experience authentic ''[[kagura]]'' dance displays with ''[[dengaku]]'' music. The Kasuga Wakamiya Festival takes place at the Wakamiya Jinja shrine from December 15 to 18th each year. The main goal of this gathering was to ward off disease while promoting new growth for the spring.{{Cite book|title=Collected writings of P.G. O'Neill = P.G.オニール論文集|last=O'Neill, P. G. |date=2001|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410506|oclc=46594973}} Like ''Kasuga Matsuri'', attendants can see kagura performances along with a procession in traditional attire. ==Kasugayama Primeval Forest== Kasugayama Primeval Forest is [[primeval forest]] of about 250 hectares (620 acres) near the summit of Kasugayama (498 metres (1,634 ft)), and contains 175 kinds of [[trees]], 60 [[bird]] types, and 1,180 species of [[insects]]. Because Kasugayama has long been tied to Kasuga Grand Shrine worship, it is regarded as a sacred hill. (Kasuga-sai: 春日祭) (13th March) | leadership = }} {{Shinto}} {{Nihongo|'''Kasuga Grand Shrine'''|春日大社|Kasuga-taisha}} is a [[Shinto shrine]] in [[Nara, Nara|Nara]], [[Nara Prefecture]], [[Japan]].Richard, Ponsonby-Fane. (1964) '' Visiting Famous Shrines in Japan,'' pp. 221-251. Established in 768 CE and rebuilt several times over the centuries, it is the shrine of the [[Fujiwara family]]. The interior is famous for its many bronze lanterns, as well as the many [[Tōrō|stone lantern]]s that lead up the shrine. The architectural style ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]]'' takes its name from Kasuga Shrine's ''[[honden]]'' (sanctuary). Kasuga Shrine, and the '''Kasugayama Primeval Forest''' near it, are registered as a [[UNESCO]] [[World Heritage Site]] as part of the "[[Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara]]". The path to Kasuga Shrine passes through a deer park. In the deer park, deer are able to roam freely and are believed to be sacred messengers of the Shinto gods that inhabit the shrine and surrounding mountainous terrain. Kasuga Shrine and the deer have been featured in several paintings and works of art of the [[Nambokucho Period]].{{cite book|last=[[Birmingham Museum of Art]]|title=Birmingham Museum of Art : guide to the collection|year=2010|publisher=Birmingham Museum of Art|location=[Birmingham, Ala]|isbn=978-1-904832-77-5|pages=46|url=http://artsbma.org}} Over three thousand stone lanterns line the way. The [[Manyo Botanical Garden, Nara|Man'yo Botanical Garden]] is adjacent to the shrine. == History == === Origin === The birth of this shrine, according to legend, began when the first kami of Kasuga-taisha, [[Takemikazuchi]], rode on the back of a white deer to the top of [[Mount Wakakusa|Mount Mikasa]] in 768 CE.{{Cite book|title=The miracles of the Kasuga deity|first=Royall|last=Tyler|date=2016|publisher=Columbia University Press|isbn=9780231534765|oclc=954193203}} This kami is said to have traveled from the [[Kashima Shrine|Kashima Jingu Shrine]] in order to protect [[Nara]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/guidance/map3/k_map01.html|title=Main Sanctuary|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} The shrine location first received favor from the Imperial government in the [[Heian period]] as a result of the power from the [[Fujiwara clan|Fujiwara family]] as well as [[Empress Shotoku]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.kasugataisha.or.jp/index.html|title=世界遺産 春日大社 公式ホームページ|website=www.kasugataisha.or.jp|access-date=2019-03-28}} From 1871 through 1946, Kasuga Shrine was officially designated one of the ''[[Modern system of ranked Shinto Shrines|Kanpei-taisha]]'' (官幣大社), meaning that it stood in the first rank of government supported shrines. == Religious significance == The four main ''[[kami]]'' enshrined here are [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]], Himegami, [[Futsunushi no Mikoto|Futsunushi no mikoto]], and [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]].{{Cite book|title=The protocol of the gods : a study of the Kasuga cult in Japanese history|author=Grapard, Allan G.|date=1992|publisher=University of California Press|isbn=0520070976|oclc=25873140}} Though these are the primary divine beings of Kasuga taisha, they are often grouped together as a [[Syncretism|syncretic,]] combined deity known as Kasuga Daimyōjin, or the "great bright kami of Kasuga."{{Cite book|title=Handbook of Japanese mythology|first=Michael|last=Ashkenazi|date=2011|publisher=ABC-CLIO|isbn=9781849728560|oclc=755870995}} This amalgam lead to the creation of the "Cult of the Kasuga" in which devotees could worship multiple kami at once. Kasuga Daimyōjin is composed of five divine beings and each consists of a [[Buddhism|Buddhist]] [[deity]] and [[Shinto]] ''[[kami]]'' counterpart. The fifth deity, Ame no oshikumone, was added much later and is said to be the divine child of [[Ame-no-Koyane|Ame no koyane]] and Himegami.{{Cite book|title=Japanese mandalas : representations of sacred geography|first=Elizabeth|last=Ten Grotenhuis|date=1999|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=0824820002|oclc=39181008}} The importance of the multifaceted kami was that it became a template for future worshipers who wanted to combine several deities to pray to at once. == Architecture == The architectural style of Kasuga-taisha comes from the name of it's main hall (''[[honden]]'') known as ''[[Kasuga-zukuri]].'' This style consists of gold and red tones that are reminiscent of Chinese architecture. The shrine complex is protected by four [[cloister]]s and contains a main sanctuary, treasure house, several different halls, and large gates. One beautiful aspect of this shrine is the many wisteria trees known as "''Sunazuri-no-Fuji''" that bloom in late April and early May. This shrine is also home to over 3,000 lanterns which are made of either stone or bronze. An entire hall is devoted to them which is ''Fujinami-no-ya'' Hall but the lanterns are only lit during the [[Setsubun|Setsubun Mantoro]] and [[Bon Festival|Chugen]] Mantoro festivals. The four main [[kami]] each have a shrine devoted to them which are all in the same [[Kasuga-zukuri|architectural style]]. They are characterized by sloping gabled roofs, a rectangular structure, [[katsuogi]] (decorative logs), and [[Chigi (architecture)|chigi]] (forked roof structures).{{Cite book|title=Shinto shrines : a guide to the sacred sites of Japan's ancient religion|first=Joseph|last=Cali|date=2013|publisher=University of Hawai'i Press|isbn=9780824837136|oclc=1043096844}} The first hall established is dedicated to [[Takemikazuchi|Takemikazuchi no mikoto]], the second to [[Futsunushi|Futsunushi no mikoto]], the third to [[Ame-no-Koyane|Amenokoyane no mikoto]], and the final hall is attributed to the consort, Himegami. Several auxillary shrines lie outside the main sanctuary that are dedicated to lesser [[kami]]. One is alloted to Tsunofuri no kami, that is commonly known as Tsubakimoto Jinja Shrine or Kayabusa Myojin. Kasenomiya Jinja Shrine is atttributed to [[Shinatsuhiko|Shinatsuhiko no mikoto]] and Shinatsuhime who are kami of the winds. Wakamiya Jinja Shrine, created in 1135 CE, is one of the more prominent auxillary shrines because it houses the ''kogami,'' or offspring kami called Ame no Oshikumono no mikoto. The primary worship here revolves around vengeful gods and the dead and is the location of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. The Treasure House at this shrine contains hundreds national treasures as well as about many other cultural properties, most of which are from the [[Heian period]]. Some of the most noteworthy items that reside here are ornate [[Taiko Drum|taiko drums]] used in [[gagaku]] from the [[Kamakura period]], arrows with crystal whistles from the [[Heian period]], and bronze mirrors of the Heian and [[Nanboku-chō period|Nanboku-cho]] periods.{{Cite web|url=https://www.tnm.jp/modules/r_free_page/index.php?id=1814&lang=en|title=Eternal Treasures from Kasugataisha Shrine|last=東京国立博物館 -トーハク-|website=www.tnm.jp|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} ==Festivals== During the festivals of ''[[Setsubun]] Mantoro'' (February 3) and ''Chugen Mantoro'' (August 14–15), three thousand shrine lanterns are all lit at once. The [[Setsubun]] Mantoro refers to the celebration of the seasonal shift from winter to spring while the [[Chugen]] Mantoro relates to the transition of summer to fall. They both takes place in order to celebrate the [[Obon]] and [[Setsubun]] holidays in Japanese culture. At Kasuga Grand shrine, people are seen writing and attaching their wishes, or [[Ema (Shinto)|''ema'']], to the lanterns before lighting them during both festivals. Additionally, it is said that tossing dried beans at these times will ward off bad luck in the future.{{Cite web|url=https://www.japan.travel/en/spot/51/|title=Setsubun Mantoro {{!}} Nara Attractions {{!}} Japan Travel {{!}} JNTO {{!}}|website=Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO)|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} March 13 is the ''Kasuga Matsuri,'' a local festival which features the dances of [[gagaku]] and [[bugaku]]. Shinto women perform traditional Japanese Yamato-mai dances that date back to the [[Heian period|Heian]] and [[Nara period]]s. This festival also holds a horse celebration which consists of a parade through the streets by a "sacred" horse.{{Cite journal|last=Smyers|first=Karen A.|last2=Bocking|first2=Brian|date=1997|title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/2385644|journal=Monumenta Nipponica|volume=52|issue=3|pages=419|doi=10.2307/2385644|issn=0027-0741}} One will see people dressed in traditional costumes of the [[Heian period|Heian]] to [[Edo period|Edo]] periods and can experience authentic ''[[kagura]]'' dance displays with ''[[dengaku]]'' music. The Kasuga Wakamiya Festival takes place at the Wakamiya Jinja shrine from December 15 to 18th each year. The main goal of this gathering was to ward off disease while promoting new growth for the spring.{{Cite book|title=Collected writings of P.G. O'Neill = P.G.オニール論文集|last=O'Neill, P. G. |date=2001|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410506|oclc=46594973}} Like ''Kasuga Matsuri'', attendants can see kagura performances along with a procession in traditional attire. ==Kasugayama Primeval Forest== Kasugayama Primeval Forest is [[primeval forest]] of about 250 hectares (620 acres) near the summit of Kasugayama (498 metres (1,634 ft)), and contains 175 kinds of [[trees]], 60 [[bird]] types, and 1,180 species of [[insects]]. In this area adjacent to Kasuga Grand Shrine, hunting and logging have been prohibited since 841 CE. Because Kasugayama has long been tied to Kasuga Grand Shrine worship, it is regarded as a sacred hill. The forest backdrop of the Kasuga Grand Shrine's buildings today has been unchanged since the [[Nara period]]. ==Images== File:Kasuga-taisha02st3200.jpg|Chakutoden File:Kasuga-taisha01bs3200.jpg|Kurumayadori File:Kasuga-taisha07bs4592.jpg|Minamimon File:Kasuga-taisha26ns3200.jpg|Sakadono File:Kasuga-taisha05n3200.jpg|''[[Heiden (Shinto)|Heiden]]'', Buden File:Kasuga-taisha25n4592.jpg|Keishoden File:Kasuga Shrine inside laterns.jpg|A smaller enclave File:Kasuga-taisha17ns4592.jpg|Lanterns File:Kasuga Grand Shrine.JPG|Corridors in the shrine complex File:Kasuga Shrine lanterns-01.jpg|Lanterns File:Bronze_lanterns,_Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Bronze lanterns File:Kasuga-taisha shrine in Nara 01.jpg|Bronze lanterns in Kasuga-taisha File:03-05-JPN129.jpg|Stone lantern leading up to shrine framing a Nara Park deer File:KasugaTaisha2.jpg|Tying [[Omikuji]] at Kasuga Shrine File:KasugaShrine.JPG|Path leading up to the shrine, braced by rows of stone lanterns File:Canberra_Nara_park.JPG|Kasuga stone lantern presented in 1997 to Nara sister city, [[Canberra, Australian Capital Territory]] File:Kasuga Shrine breast plaques.jpg|A "breast shrine" at the Kasuga Shrine walk decked with [[Ema (Shinto)|Ema]] plaques File:2018 Ichi-no-Torii of Kasuga-taisha.jpg|Ichi-no-[[Torii]] file:Armour red threads Kasuga shrine.jpg|Armour laced with red threads With bamboo, tiger, sparrow motif; nomination includes the helmet; said to have been dedicated by Minamoto no Yoshitsune; one of two similar armours at Kasuga-taisha 1185　Kamakura period Ō-yoroi File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 01.jpg|Hanging lanterns and Andons in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival File:Setsubun Mantoro Festival 20150203 09.jpg|Hanging lanterns and [[Traditional lighting equipment of Japan#Andon|Andon]]s in the Setsubun Mantoro Festival. Wakamiya Jinja Shrine, created in 1135 CE, is one of the more prominent auxillary shrines because it houses the ''kogami,'' or offspring kami called Ame no Oshikumono no mikoto. The primary worship here revolves around vengeful gods and the dead and is the location of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival. Some of the most noteworthy items that reside here are ornate [[Taiko Drum|taiko drums]] used in [[gagaku]] from the [[Kamakura period]], arrows with crystal whistles from the [[Heian period]], and bronze mirrors of the Heian and [[Nanboku-chō period|Nanboku-cho]] periods.{{Cite web|url=https://www.tnm.jp/modules/r_free_page/index.php?id=1814&lang=en|title=Eternal Treasures from Kasugataisha Shrine|last=東京国立博物館 -トーハク-|website=www.tnm.jp|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} ==Festivals== During the festivals of ''[[Setsubun]] Mantoro'' (February 3) and ''Chugen Mantoro'' (August 14–15), three thousand shrine lanterns are all lit at once. At Kasuga Grand shrine, people are seen writing and attaching their wishes, or [[Ema (Shinto)|''ema'']], to the lanterns before lighting them during both festivals. Additionally, it is said that tossing dried beans at these times will ward off bad luck in the future.{{Cite web|url=https://www.japan.travel/en/spot/51/|title=Setsubun Mantoro {{!}} Nara Attractions {{!}} Japan Travel {{!}} JNTO {{!}}|website=Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO)|language=en|access-date=2019-04-08}} March 13 is the ''Kasuga Matsuri,'' a local festival which features the dances of [[gagaku]] and [[bugaku]]. G. |date=2001|publisher=Japan Library|isbn=1873410506|oclc=46594973}} Like ''Kasuga Matsuri'', attendants can see kagura performances along with a procession in traditional attire. ==Kasugayama Primeval Forest== Kasugayama Primeval Forest is [[primeval forest]] of about 250 hectares (620 acres) near the summit of Kasugayama (498 metres (1,634 ft)), and contains 175 kinds of [[trees]], 60 [[bird]] types, and 1,180 species of [[insects]].
